title: The Guest Star: July 1054
subtitle: The supernova that left the Crab Nebula, seen from Kaifeng, the Liao court, Kyoto and Constantinople, and traced back nine centuries later
span: 1054–1056 (with records copied to c.1270 and identified 1731–1942)
intro: Before dawn on 4 July 1054 (Julian), astronomers of the Song court at Kaifeng logged a new star a few inches, in their angular measure, from Tianguan, the star now called zeta Tauri, at the tip of the Bull's southern horn. For twenty-three days it could be seen in full daylight, as bright as Venus, with points of light on four sides and a reddish-white colour. By night it lingered for almost two years, until the bureau reported on 6 April 1056 that the 'guest' had left. The star had exploded about 6,500 light years away; its debris is the Crab Nebula, and the collapsed core at its centre was found in 1968 to be a pulsar spinning about thirty times a second.

This chapter is unusual in Many Eyes because almost none of its eyes is a diary in the modern sense. The East Asian records are official astronomical and court documents, and most survive only inside compilations made long afterwards: the Song shi was compiled in 1343–45, the Song huiyao survives as a nineteenth-century reconstruction, the Liao record sits in a thirteenth-century history of the Khitan, and the Japanese entries were copied from the archive of the Onmyōryō (the court Bureau of Yin and Yang) into Fujiwara no Teika's diary in 1230 and into the chronicle Ichidai yōki. The one possible witness from the Mediterranean, the physician Ibn Butlan, is known only through a biographical dictionary compiled two centuries later. Each eye's form and authenticity notes say plainly what kind of record it is and how it reached us.

The records disagree in instructive ways. The Japanese texts put the star in the fourth month, which would place it in May, when Taurus was lost in the Sun's glare; most scholars read this as a copying error for the fifth month. One Chinese compilation gives the day as yichou instead of jichou, which would move the first sighting to 10 June. A Liao text links the star to a solar eclipse and to the death of the Khitan emperor. A minority of modern researchers have argued from European and Near Eastern texts that the star appeared in April or May, earlier than the Chinese date; others reject every European candidate. In the American Southwest, a painted hand, crescent and star below the Peñasco Blanco great house in Chaco Canyon has been read since 1955 as a record of the star beside the waning Moon on 5 July 1054, and is also firmly doubted. These are laid out here as positions, not settled facts.

Twelve days after the first sighting, on Saturday 16 July 1054, the papal legate Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida walked into Hagia Sophia in Constantinople and laid a bull excommunicating Patriarch Michael Cerularius on the altar. If the Chinese date is right, the guest star was then still visible in the daytime sky above the city. No Greek or Latin writer of the schism mentions it. Ibn Butlan, who was in Constantinople that year and had written a treatise on the Eucharist for the patriarch's circle, is the only person known to have stood in that city and also written about the star.

The second half of the story is the identification chain, flagged throughout as later. John Bevis saw a faint nebula near zeta Tauri around 1731; Charles Messier, hunting for the predicted return of Halley's comet, found it in August–September 1758 and made it the first entry in his catalogue of objects that were not comets. Lord Rosse drew it in 1844 with a shape that gave it the name Crab. In 1921 Knut Lundmark noticed that a Chinese guest star of 1054 had been recorded close to it; in 1928 Edwin Hubble argued that its measured expansion implied an age of about nine centuries; and in 1942 the sinologist J. J. L. Duyvendak, with Nicholas Mayall and Jan Oort, published the translations and astronomical analysis that made the link between the 1054 star and the nebula the standard case of a supernova and its remnant.
calendar_note: All date_iso values for 1054–1056 are proleptic Julian dates, as historians and astronomers cite them; the Gregorian equivalent in the eleventh century is six days later (Julian 4 July 1054 = Gregorian 10 July). The Song record dates the first sighting to the Zhihe era, 1st year, 5th lunar month, on the day jichou: Chinese days are counted in a continuous sixty-day cycle independent of the month, and jichou (day 26 of the cycle) in that month falls on 4 July 1054. A later variant, yichou (day 2 of the cycle), would fall on 10 June; most scholars treat it as a scribal slip between similar characters. Yang Weide's memorial is dated Zhihe 1, 7th month, 22nd day = 27 August 1054. The disappearance report is dated in the next era, Jiayou 1, 3rd month, on the day xinwei = 6 April 1056, about 642 days after the first sighting. Japanese court dates use era names (nengō) and lunar months: Tengi 2, 4th month, 'middle decade' (days 11–20) corresponds roughly to mid- to late May 1054; read as the 5th month it falls in late June, still somewhat before 4 July, so the Japanese date is shown as a range and marked approximate. Teika's own entry is dated Kanki 2, 11th month, 8th day (late 1230; the exact Julian day is not confirmed here and is given to the month). Ibn Butlan's year 446 of the Hijra ran from about 12 April 1054 to 1 April 1055; the text also gives 445, which began in April 1053. European dates are Julian as written; Pope Leo IX died on 19 April 1054. The Liao record uses the Khitan reign era Chongxi; Emperor Xingzong died in its 24th year, on 28 August 1055 (Julian).

eyes.name: Astronomical Bureau of the Song court (Sitiandian / Sitianjian)
eyes.role: Imperial office of astronomers who watched the sky nightly, logged portents and reported them to Emperor Renzong (r. 1022–1063)
eyes.vantage_label: court astronomers who watched the star itself
eyes.form: official astronomical records (surviving in later compilations)
eyes.authenticity: No original Song observing log survives. The records are preserved in the Song shi (official dynastic history, compiled 1343–45 under the Yuan), its astronomical treatise and basic annals; in the Song huiyao (collected documents of the Song, whose surviving text is the Song huiyao jigao reconstructed in the nineteenth century from the Ming Yongle dadian); in Ma Duanlin's Wenxian tongkao (c.1300); and in Li Tao's Xu zizhi tongjian changbian (twelfth century), which gives the variant day yichou. These are faithful-looking copies of bureau reports, but every surviving word is later transmission.
eyes.bio: The Song state treated the sky as a mirror of government, so its astronomers measured and dated anything new and wrote it up with an interpretation. Their notes on the 1054 star give the position relative to Tianguan, its daylight visibility, colour and the day it vanished, figures precise enough that nine centuries later they could be matched to a nebula and an expansion age.

sources.title: Translations of the Song shi and Song huiyao records (University of Colorado course page, after Duyvendak 1942)
History of Song, astronomy treatise (Chinese text, chinesenotes.com)

eyes.name: Yang Weide
eyes.role: Senior court astronomer and director of the astronomical office under Emperor Renzong; author of works on calendrical and divinatory astronomy
eyes.vantage_label: the astronomer who turned the star into an omen
eyes.form: memorial to the throne (preserved in the Song huiyao)
eyes.authenticity: His memorial of 27 August 1054 survives only as quoted in the Song huiyao (ch. 52 of the astronomy section in the reconstructed jigao); its wording is consistent across modern translations, beginning with Duyvendak's in 1942.
eyes.bio: Yang Weide's report shows what the star meant at court rather than what it looked like. Reading it against the old divination manuals, he found it auspicious, a sign of a person of great worth in the realm, and asked that his memorial be sent to the historians. It is the only eleventh-century text that names the person who interpreted the star.

sources.title: Song huiyao translation including Yang Weide's memorial

eyes.name: Liao (Khitan) court record, as preserved in the Qidan guozhi
eyes.life: record c.1054–55; compilation attributed to Ye Longli, 1247
eyes.role: Record of portents at the court of the Khitan Liao emperor Xingzong (r. 1031–1055)
eyes.side: Liao (Qidan) empire, northern China and Mongolia
eyes.where: The itinerant Liao court; placed here at the Supreme Capital, Shangjing
eyes.authenticity: The Qidan guozhi ('Record of the Khitan State') is attributed to the Southern Song author Ye Longli and dated 1247; its authorship and date have themselves been questioned. Its entry places a guest star in the lunar lodge Mao (the Pleiades) in the year before Xingzong's death and links it to a midday solar eclipse. The translation and dating are disputed (see the observing ledger). Treat as a later, secondhand record.
eyes.bio: The Liao were the Song dynasty's great northern rival, paid an annual subsidy by the Song under the treaty of 1005. That their own court tradition apparently noted the same star shows it was watched in two competing capitals at once, and read in each as a sign about its own ruler.

sources.title: Summary of the Qidan guozhi entry and its debated reading (mirror of an encyclopedia article on SN 1054)
Collins, Claspy and Martin, 'A reinterpretation of historical references to the supernova of A.D. 1054', PASP 111 (1999)

eyes.name: Fujiwara no Teika (Sadaie)
eyes.role: Court noble and poet, compiler of imperial anthologies; aged 68 when he made the entry, in 1230
eyes.vantage_label: a diarist copying the court archive 176 years later
eyes.form: diary (entry of 1230 quoting earlier official records)
eyes.authenticity: Teika's diary Meigetsuki survives largely in his own hand (the Reizei family holding is a National Treasure). The list of past guest stars appears in the entry for Kanki 2, 11th month, 8th day (1230); it was supplied by the Onmyōryō official Abe no Yasutoshi and appears to be a separate sheet joined into the diary, so it is the bureau's text, not Teika's own observation.
eyes.bio: When a new 'guest star' (actually a comet) appeared in late 1230, Teika asked the court diviner Abe no Yasutoshi for precedents. The eight cases he received include the stars of 1006, 1054 and 1181, all now known supernovae. Teika never saw the 1054 star; his diary is the reason the Japanese record survives.

sources.title: Kyoto Computer Gakuin, 'Meigetsuki' guest-star article (Japanese PDF, gives the 1054 passage)
Kwasan Observatory article on the Meigetsuki guest-star list and Abe no Yasutoshi (Japanese PDF)

eyes.name: Compiler of the Ichidai yōki
eyes.role: Anonymous compiler of a chronicle of the reigns of Japanese emperors
eyes.vantage_label: a chronicler copying the same archive
eyes.authenticity: The Ichidai yōki entry for 1054 is nearly identical to the Meigetsuki text. Because its guest-star list ends with a case of 1166, Japanese scholars think it was copied from the Onmyōryō's records on another occasion, not from Teika's diary. Like the Meigetsuki, it gives the 4th month.
eyes.bio: A second, independent copy of the Japanese bureau's note matters because it shows the 'fourth month' was already in the archive both copyists used, rather than a slip by Teika.

sources.title: Kwasan Observatory article discussing the Ichidai yōki record (Japanese PDF)

eyes.name: Abu al-Hasan al-Mukhtar ibn Butlan
eyes.role: Christian (Church of the East) physician from Baghdad, later author of the Taqwim al-sihha; travelling and practising medicine
eyes.side: Abbasid and Fatimid worlds; a guest in Byzantine Constantinople
eyes.vantage_label: a foreign physician in the city of the schism
eyes.form: medical writing on epidemics (preserved only in a later biographical dictionary)
eyes.authenticity: His words survive only as quoted by Ibn Abi Usaybi'a (1203–1270) in his biographical dictionary of physicians, 'Uyun al-anba' fi tabaqat al-atibba', about two hundred years later. The passage was brought to astronomers' attention in 1978 (Brecher, Lieber and Lieber, Nature). It gives the year as both 445 and 446 of the Hijra, so its exact date is uncertain.
eyes.bio: Ibn Butlan had argued publicly with the Egyptian physician Ibn Ridwan in Fustat before travelling to Constantinople, where he wrote on the Eucharist for the circle of Patriarch Cerularius in the months before the schism. In a discussion of epidemics he recalled that a famous outbreak came when 'the spectacular star' appeared in Gemini. He is the only known writer to place the star over Constantinople, and he linked it with disease, not with the quarrel of the churches.

sources.title: Was the Supernova of 1054 CE Recorded in Constantinople? (Digilec / DMAE, Universidad Complutense)
Ibn Butlan (encyclopedia mirror)

eyes.name: Anonymous author of the Tractatus de ecclesia S. Petri Aldenburgensi
eyes.life: written later than 1054; date of composition uncertain
eyes.role: Monastic writer of the abbey of St Peter at Oudenburg, Flanders, recording the death of Pope Leo IX
eyes.where: Event placed at Rome; text written at Oudenburg

waypoints.label: Oudenburg, where the text was written

eyes.authenticity: The passage describes a bright orb at the hour of Leo IX's death on 19 April 1054. Collins, Claspy and Martin (1999) proposed it as a European record of the supernova, seen in the evening sky before the Chinese date. Most specialists, including Stephenson and Green, regard it as vague, conventional saintly imagery or a planet, and do not accept it. Shown only as a disputed position.
eyes.bio: This text belongs here as the best-known of the contested European candidates, together with the Rampona chronicle of Bologna and an Irish annal entry of 1054. It also links the sky to the schism: Leo IX was the pope who sent Humbert to Constantinople, and his death in April left the legates acting for a dead man.

sources.title: Collins, Claspy and Martin (1999), PASP 111: 871–880
European historical evidence of the supernova of AD 1054 (arXiv 2103.13290)

eyes.name: Unknown Ancestral Puebloan painter(s) of the Peñasco Blanco panel
eyes.life: painting undated; Chaco great houses occupied c.850–1150
eyes.role: Painter of a hand, a crescent and a rayed star on a cliff overhang below the Peñasco Blanco great house
eyes.where: Peñasco Blanco, west end of Chaco Canyon, New Mexico
eyes.vantage_label: a possible eyewitness on another continent (contested)
eyes.authenticity: The panel has no date and no text. William C. Miller (1955) first proposed that crescent-and-star rock art in northern Arizona depicted the 1054 star beside the waning Moon; the Peñasco Blanco panel later became the best-known example. E. C. Krupp (2015) argues that its style resembles later Zuni imagery and that none of the star-and-crescent images is a satisfactory record of the supernova. The interpretation is uncertain.
eyes.bio: Including this panel shows how a record without words is read. If the Chacoans did see the star, they would have seen it rise before dawn next to the old crescent Moon in early July; if they did not, the panel may be a sun-watching station marker or later sacred imagery. Both readings are given here.

sources.title: National Park Service, Chaco Culture: Petroglyphs and Pictographs
High Altitude Observatory, Supernova Pictograph
E. C. Krupp, 'Crab supernova rock art', Journal of Skyscape Archaeology 1.2 (2015)

eyes.name: Humbert of Silva Candida
eyes.role: Cardinal-bishop of Silva Candida, leader of the papal legation sent by Leo IX to Constantinople in 1054
eyes.vantage_label: on the same ground, looking at the altar not the sky
eyes.form: narrative of the legation and dated bull of excommunication
eyes.authenticity: Humbert's own account, the Brevis et succincta commemoratio, and the text of the bull survive and are edited (Will, Acta et scripta, 1861). They are partisan documents written to justify the legation.
eyes.bio: Humbert was the reforming papacy's sharpest polemicist. His account of the summer of 1054 gives the days of the debate, the bull and the departure; nothing in it mentions a new star, although if the Chinese date is right it was visible in daylight over the city.

sources.title: Humbert of Silva Candida (encyclopedia article)
The days of the schism of 1054 (chronology)

eyes.name: Michael I Cerularius (Keroularios)
eyes.where: Constantinople, the patriarchate at Hagia Sophia
eyes.vantage_label: on the same ground, the excommunicated patriarch
eyes.authenticity: The synodal edict of July 1054 and his letters to Patriarch Peter III of Antioch survive and are edited (Will, Acta et scripta, 1861). Like Humbert's texts they are partisan; later Byzantine historians barely mention the events.
eyes.bio: Cerularius answered the bull with a synod that anathematized the legates and with letters justifying himself to the other Eastern patriarchs. His documents, like Humbert's, are silent about the sky.

sources.title: Michael I Cerularius (encyclopedia article)
Rethinking the Schism of 1054 (Cambridge, PDF)

eyes.name: Charles Messier
eyes.role: Astronomer of the French Navy, aged 28 in 1758, searching for the predicted return of Halley's comet
eyes.where: Observatory in the tower of the Hôtel de Cluny, Paris
eyes.vantage_label: later: first to catalogue the remnant
eyes.authenticity: His catalogue, first published in the Mémoires of the Académie royale des sciences for 1771 (issued 1774), gives the observation date of 12 September 1758 for the first entry; his notes indicate he first saw it in late August 1758. He credited John Bevis's earlier sighting (c.1731).
eyes.bio: Messier did not know the nebula had a history. Mistaking it at first for a comet, he decided to list such fixed fuzzy objects so comet hunters would not be fooled. That is why the remnant of the 1054 star is M1.

sources.title: Messier 1 (M1), the Crab Nebula (Universe Today)

eyes.name: William Parsons, 3rd Earl of Rosse
eyes.vantage_label: later: gave the nebula its name
eyes.authenticity: His 1844 drawing of M1, made with a 36-inch reflector, was published in the Philosophical Transactions; it is the source of the name 'Crab'. His later drawings with the 72-inch 'Leviathan' look less crab-like.
eyes.bio: Rosse's large reflectors showed filaments that earlier observers could not see. The crab-like sketch fixed the popular name of the nebula long before anyone knew it was the debris of the 1054 star.

sources.title: Messier 1, history of observation (Universe Today)

eyes.name: Knut Lundmark
eyes.side: Sweden (working in Uppsala and at US observatories)
eyes.authenticity: 'Suspected new stars recorded in the old chronicles and among recent meridian observations', Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific 33 (1921): 225ff. A list compiled from earlier European translations of Chinese records.
eyes.bio: Lundmark's list of guest stars from Chinese chronicles noted, almost in passing, that the star of 1054 had stood near the nebula NGC 1952 (M1). It was the first printed link between the record and the remnant.

sources.title: Summary of the identification chain (encyclopedia mirror)

eyes.name: Edwin Powell Hubble
eyes.role: Astronomer at Mount Wilson Observatory, aged 38–39
eyes.authenticity: 'Novae or temporary stars', Astronomical Society of the Pacific Leaflet no. 14 (1928). Short popular article; the age estimate relied on expansion measurements made by J. C. Duncan and others in 1921.
eyes.bio: Hubble took the observed expansion of the nebula's filaments, ran it backwards, and found that the nebula would have been a point about 900 years before, matching the Chinese guest star of 1054. Later measurements show the expansion has accelerated, so the simple back-calculation gives a date somewhat after 1054.

sources.title: Benchmarks: July 4, 1054 (Earth magazine)

eyes.name: Nicholas U. Mayall and Jan H. Oort (with J. J. L. Duyvendak)
eyes.role: Lick Observatory spectroscopist; Leiden astronomer; Leiden sinologist
eyes.authenticity: Mayall, 'The Crab Nebula, a probable supernova', ASP Leaflet no. 119 (1939); Duyvendak, 'Further data bearing on the identification of the Crab Nebula with the supernova of 1054 A.D. Part I. The ancient oriental chronicles', PASP 54 (1942): 91–94; Mayall and Oort, 'Part II. The astronomical aspects', PASP 54 (1942): 95–104. Published in occupied-Netherlands wartime conditions for the Leiden authors.
eyes.bio: Oort asked his Leiden colleague Duyvendak to re-translate every Chinese source, and with Mayall used the daylight visibility, distance and expansion to show that the star had been a supernova, far brighter than an ordinary nova. Their two papers are the reason the Song bureau's notes are now cited in astrophysics.

sources.title: J. J. L. Duyvendak (encyclopedia article)
Song records as translated after Duyvendak

entries.headline: A Baghdad physician spars with Cairo's medical establishment
entries.digest: Before he reached Constantinople, Ibn Butlan spent several years in Fatimid Egypt, where he and the physician Ibn Ridwan exchanged polemical treatises in a famous quarrel of physicians. Epidemics, the Nile flood and the causes of disease were the shared concerns of both men, and they frame how Ibn Butlan later remembered the star.
entries.source_note: Ibn Butlan biography (encyclopedia mirror); dates of the Egyptian stay are approximate.

entries.headline: Papal legates arrive to settle the quarrel with the patriarch
entries.digest: Humbert, with the papal chancellor Frederick of Lorraine and Archbishop Peter of Amalfi, reached Constantinople bearing letters from Pope Leo IX. Emperor Constantine IX received them well; Patriarch Cerularius, offended by their manner and their letters, refused to treat them as superiors. The legates did not yet know that the pope who had sent them was dying.
entries.source_note: Humbert's Commemoratio as summarized in modern accounts; arrival month approximate.

entries.headline: Writing on the Eucharist for the patriarch's circle
entries.digest: In the months before the break, Ibn Butlan composed a treatise on the Eucharist, the disputed question of leavened against unleavened bread, at the instance of people around Cerularius. A Baghdad Christian physician thus became a minor player in the Greek case against the Latins, in the same city and season as Humbert's legation.
entries.source_note: arXiv 2103.13290, which dates the essay to March–May 1054; see also the DMAE (Complutense) study.

entries.place: Rome (as reported in a Flemish text)
entries.headline: An orb of light at the hour of Pope Leo IX's death
entries.digest: The Oudenburg text says that at the very hour Leo IX died, an orb of extraordinary brilliance appeared. Collins, Claspy and Martin read this as the supernova in the evening sky, months before the Chinese first sighting; most specialists treat it as a vague, conventional sign of sanctity, or a planet, since Venus and other bright objects were in the western sky. The date of the death is firm; the star is not.
entries.source_note: Collins, Claspy and Martin (1999), PASP 111; Leo IX's death 19 April 1054.

entries.date_display: Tengi 2, 4th month, middle decade (c. mid- to late May 1054), at the hour of the ox
entries.headline: Bureau record: a guest star in the east, as large as Jupiter
entries.digest: The precedent list in Teika's diary says that in the reign of Go-Reizei, after the middle of the 4th month of Tengi 2, around 2 a.m., a guest star came out in the degrees of the lodges Shi and Shen (in Orion), seen in the east, and flared at Tianguan; it was as large as Jupiter. Japanese astronomers note that in the 4th month Taurus lay close to the Sun and could not have been seen before dawn, so the month is probably an error for the 5th.
entries.source_note: Meigetsuki, Kanki 2/11/8 entry; Japanese text quoted in the Kyoto Computer Gakuin PDF; Kwasan Observatory article.

entries.place: Kyoto (the event; copied in the 13th century)
entries.headline: A second copy of the same Japanese note
entries.digest: The Ichidai yōki chronicle gives almost the same words: a guest star in the degrees of Shi and Shen, flaring at Tianguan, in the 4th month of Tengi 2. Because it seems to have been copied separately from the bureau archive, the shared 'fourth month' points to an error already present in the Onmyōryō's records.
entries.source_note: Kwasan Observatory article on the Ichidai yōki and Meigetsuki lists.

entries.headline: A guest star in the Pleiades during a midday eclipse?
entries.digest: The Qidan guozhi entry, set before the death of the Khitan emperor Xingzong, says a guest star appeared in the lodge Mao during a solar eclipse at noon. One translation takes this to mean the star was seen during the eclipse of 10 May 1054; Breen and McCarthy instead date the sighting to January 1055, and others connect the eclipse to 13 November 1053 and treat the star as a separate note. The entry probably refers to the 1054 star, but the day cannot be fixed.
entries.source_note: Collins et al. (1999) summarizing Ho et al. (1972) and Breen and McCarthy (1995); encyclopedia mirror summary.

entries.headline: The spectacular star in Gemini and the year's epidemic
entries.digest: Writing on epidemics, Ibn Butlan recalled that one of the famous outbreaks of his time came when the spectacular star appeared in Gemini, in the year 446. He described mass deaths in Constantinople, with some fourteen thousand buried in one church after the cemeteries filled, and an outbreak in Egypt as well. He treats the star as a sign accompanying corruption of the air, not as a political omen. The passage survives only through Ibn Abi Usaybi'a, and its 445/446 inconsistency leaves the exact timing open.
entries.source_note: Ibn Abi Usaybi'a, 'Uyun al-anba', as discussed in Collins et al. (1999), arXiv 2103.13290 and the DMAE study; figure of 14,000 from these summaries.

entries.headline: A Greek monk retracts before the emperor
entries.digest: In the debates over unleavened bread, clerical marriage and the Creed, Humbert wrote a sharp reply to the Studite monk Niketas Stethatos, who had attacked Latin practice. Under imperial pressure Niketas withdrew his treatise, and Humbert recorded it as a victory; Cerularius stayed out of reach.
entries.source_note: Humbert's Commemoratio as summarized in modern studies; month approximate.

entries.date_display: Zhihe 1, 5th month, day yichou (= 10 June 1054) — variant
entries.headline: A variant day: yichou instead of jichou
entries.digest: Li Tao's Xu zizhi tongjian changbian gives the first-sighting day as yichou, which would fall on 10 June, more than three weeks earlier than the other Song texts. Most scholars treat the difference as a copying slip between two similar characters and keep 4 July; a few have used it to argue for an earlier appearance.
entries.source_note: Encyclopedia mirror summary of the jichou/yichou issue.

entries.headline: Writing to Peter of Antioch to justify himself
entries.digest: Cerularius sent the patriarch Peter III of Antioch an account of the affair and a list of Latin errors, seeking eastern support. Peter's reply urged moderation and separated serious matters from customs he thought tolerable. The exchange shows the quarrel being argued by letter across the eastern patriarchates.
entries.source_note: Letters edited in Will, Acta et scripta (1861); summarized in modern studies. Dating approximate.

entries.date_display: Zhihe 1, 5th month, day jichou (4 July 1054, Julian), before dawn
entries.headline: A guest star appears beside Tianguan
entries.digest: The bureau recorded a guest star some inches (a small angular measure) to the south-east of Tianguan, zeta Tauri, at the southern horn of the Bull, seen in the east at dawn. Modern work shows that 'south-east' here follows a convention for a star standing on guard below its reference star; the Crab Nebula lies about a degree from zeta Tauri.
entries.source_note: Song shi, astronomical treatise ch. 56; Song huiyao; translations on the JILA page.

entries.headline: Seen in broad daylight, like Venus
entries.digest: The Song huiyao adds that the star could be seen in the daytime like Venus, with pointed rays on all four sides and a reddish-white colour, and that it remained visible by day for twenty-three days in all. Modern astronomers take the twenty-three days as the span of daylight visibility, with nighttime sightings continuing much longer.
entries.source_note: Song huiyao (jigao), as translated on the JILA page.

entries.headline: Before dawn, the star beside the old crescent Moon
entries.digest: On this morning a thin waning crescent Moon stood about two degrees from the new star, low in the eastern sky before sunrise, according to William Miller's 1955 calculation. Supporters read the Peñasco Blanco panel's crescent, ten-rayed star and hand as a record of that sight. Critics note that the panel is undated, that its style may be centuries later, and that the crescent-and-star pairing is common in Pueblo imagery for other reasons.
entries.source_note: Krupp (2015), summarizing Miller (1955); NPS Chaco petroglyphs page. The sky is calculated; the painting's date is unknown.

entries.headline: The bull of excommunication laid on the altar
entries.digest: Shortly before the Divine Liturgy, Humbert and his fellow legates walked into the sanctuary of Hagia Sophia and placed a bull excommunicating Cerularius and his supporters on the altar. Leaving, they shook the dust from their feet and called on God to see and judge. If the Chinese date is right, the guest star was still visible by day above the city twelve days after its first sighting.
entries.source_note: Humbert's Commemoratio; chronology page 'The days of the schism of 1054'.

entries.headline: Day thirteen of daylight visibility
entries.digest: By the Song bureau's count the star was still visible by day on this date, the thirteenth of its twenty-three days. No Song record mentions the West; the observers had no knowledge of the Latin and Greek churches or their quarrel.
entries.source_note: Computed from the Song huiyao's 23 days counted from 4 July; not itself a dated entry.

entries.headline: The legates leave, are recalled, and do not meet the patriarch
entries.digest: Two days after the bull, the legates set out for Rome with the emperor's gifts. Constantine IX called them back from Selymbria to meet Cerularius, but the meeting the patriarch proposed in Hagia Sophia never took place, and the legates sailed. Riots in the city followed.
entries.source_note: Humbert's Commemoratio as summarized in modern accounts; day approximate.

entries.headline: A synod anathematizes the legates
entries.digest: Four days after the bull, Cerularius assembled a synod which condemned the document and anathematized its authors. The synodal edict presented the legates as impostors acting without proper papal authority, and blamed them, not the Roman see, for the insult.
entries.source_note: Edictum synodale (Will, Acta et scripta); chronology page 'The days of the schism of 1054'.

entries.headline: The anathema is read in Hagia Sophia
entries.digest: The synod's anathema was proclaimed publicly in the Great Church. Contemporary Byzantine historians such as Psellos and Attaliates passed over the whole affair; only later did 1054 become the conventional date of a great schism.
entries.source_note: Chronology page 'The days of the schism of 1054'.

entries.headline: The star fades out of the daytime sky
entries.digest: Counting twenty-three days from 4 July, the star dropped below daylight visibility at about this date, but stayed visible before dawn and at night. This is a calculated end point, not a dated record.
entries.source_note: Calculated from the Song huiyao's 23 days.

entries.headline: The star read as a favourable omen
entries.digest: Yang Weide memorialized that he had seen the guest star, with a faint yellow glow about it. Following the divination texts, he judged that because it did not trespass on the lodge Bi and its light was full, it signified a person of great worth in the realm, and he asked that his report be handed to the historians. The officials offered their congratulations.
entries.source_note: Song huiyao, as translated on the JILA page.

entries.headline: The memorial is sent to the history office
entries.digest: The emperor ordered Yang's memorial passed to the Bureau of Historiography, which is how the report entered the records that later compilers used. The same day's notice therefore shows both the observation and the political use of it.
entries.source_note: Song huiyao, as translated on the JILA page.

entries.headline: Death of the Khitan emperor after the omen
entries.digest: The Liao emperor Xingzong died. The Qidan guozhi sets its guest-star entry before this death, reading the star as a warning to the Khitan ruler, the reverse of the Song astronomer's favourable reading in Kaifeng.
entries.source_note: Encyclopedia mirror summary of the Qidan guozhi entry; date of death as given there.

entries.date_display: Jiayou 1, 3rd month, day xinwei (6 April 1056, Julian)
entries.headline: The guest departs
entries.digest: The director of the astronomical bureau reported that the guest star, seen since the 5th month of Zhihe 1 at dawn in the east guarding Tianguan, could no longer be seen. He called it an omen of the departure of the guest. Counting from 4 July 1054 it had been visible for about 642 days.
entries.source_note: Song shi basic annals; Song huiyao; JILA translations; 642-day figure from arXiv 2103.13290.

entries.headline: A comet sends Teika looking for precedents
entries.digest: When a new guest star appeared on the 1st day of the 11th month, Teika, ever anxious about omens, asked the Onmyōryō official Abe no Yasutoshi what precedents existed. The object of 1230 was in fact a comet.
entries.source_note: KCG Meigetsuki PDF; Julian month approximate.

entries.headline: Eight precedents copied into the diary
entries.digest: At the end of this day's entry the diary carries a list of eight earlier guest stars supplied by Yasutoshi, including those of 1006, 1054 and 1181. The sheet appears to be the bureau's own text joined into the diary, so it is Teika's record of the archive rather than his own words about 1054.
entries.source_note: Kwasan Observatory article (entry date Kanki 2/11/8); exact Julian day not confirmed, precision kept to the month in date_iso.

entries.headline: A fuzzy patch that is not the comet
entries.digest: While searching for the predicted return of Halley's comet, Messier found a faint nebulous patch above the southern horn of Taurus and at first took it for a comet. It did not move. He resolved to list such objects so that comet hunters would not confuse them.
entries.source_note: Universe Today, Messier 1; day from Messier's notes as summarized there.

entries.headline: Position measured: the first object in the catalogue
entries.digest: Messier measured the nebula's position and later described it as containing no star, a whitish light shaped like a candle flame. It became number 1 of his catalogue; he noted that the English observer John Bevis had seen it about 1731.
entries.source_note: Messier's catalogue entry for M1 as quoted in Universe Today.

entries.headline: The catalogue goes to press
entries.digest: Messier's first list of nebulae and star clusters appeared in the Academy's Mémoires. M1 was there with its position, still with no idea that it marked the place of a star seen in 1054.
entries.source_note: Standard bibliography of the Messier catalogue.

entries.headline: A drawing that looks like a crab
entries.digest: With his 36-inch reflector Rosse drew M1 as an oval with trailing filaments like legs or claws, and the name Crab Nebula followed from the drawing. His later drawings with the 72-inch Leviathan, which showed more detail, looked much less like a crab, but the name stuck.
entries.source_note: Universe Today, Messier 1; year of the drawing as given there.

entries.headline: Looking again with the Leviathan
entries.digest: Rosse and his assistants re-observed the nebula with the larger telescope, recording more of its filamentary structure. The nebula was a curiosity of nebular astronomy; nobody yet asked how old it was.
entries.source_note: Universe Today, Messier 1 (1848 re-observation).

entries.headline: Lundmark notices the 1054 star sat near M1
entries.digest: In a list of suspected new stars drawn from Chinese chronicles, Lundmark noted that the guest star of 1054 had been recorded close to the nebula NGC 1952. In the same year Carl Lampland and John Duncan showed from photographs that the nebula was changing and expanding.
entries.source_note: Lundmark, PASP 33 (1921); encyclopedia mirror summary.

entries.headline: Running the expansion backwards gives about 900 years
entries.digest: In a popular leaflet on novae, Hubble argued that the measured expansion of the Crab implied it had started from a point around nine centuries earlier, and that it was the remains of the 1054 guest star. He proposed the link without detailed study of the Chinese texts.
entries.source_note: Earth magazine Benchmarks; Hubble, ASP Leaflet no. 14 (1928).

entries.headline: A supernova, not an ordinary nova
entries.digest: Mayall argued in an ASP leaflet that the Crab's expansion speed and the brightness the Chinese reported meant the 1054 star had been a supernova, a far more energetic event than an ordinary nova.
entries.source_note: Earth magazine Benchmarks (Mayall's 1939 leaflet).

entries.headline: Duyvendak translates the Song records afresh
entries.digest: At Oort's request, the Leiden sinologist Duyvendak gathered and re-translated the Song shi, Song huiyao and related records, including Yang Weide's memorial and the 1056 disappearance report. His translations, published as Part I, remain the basis of most later English versions.
entries.source_note: Duyvendak, PASP 54 (1942): 91–94; JILA page (translations after Duyvendak).

entries.headline: The astronomical case closes
entries.digest: In Part II, Mayall and Oort combined the daylight visibility, the 642-day span, the nebula's distance and its expansion to show that the 1054 star had reached a brightness only a supernova could explain. The paper made the Crab the textbook link between a dated historical star and its remnant.
entries.source_note: Mayall and Oort, PASP 54 (1942): 95–104.

entries.headline: A rock-art reading is proposed
entries.digest: William C. Miller of Mount Wilson and Palomar proposed that crescent-and-star paintings at White Mesa and Navaho Canyon in Arizona showed the 1054 star beside the waning Moon. The idea spread to the Peñasco Blanco panel at Chaco, which became its best-known example.
entries.source_note: Krupp (2015), summarizing Miller (1955).

entries.headline: A catalogue of twenty-one candidate sites
entries.digest: John Brandt and Ray Williamson compiled a catalogue of 21 possible supernova rock-art sites across the Southwest. Critics later argued that the criteria were loose: crescents facing the wrong way and sites with no eastern view were included.
entries.source_note: Krupp (2015).

entries.headline: The rock-art identification is rejected in detail
entries.digest: E. C. Krupp reviewed the sites one by one and concluded that none of the main star-and-crescent images is a satisfactory record of the 1054 star. He judged Peñasco Blanco stylistically closer to later Zuni imagery and the 'poster child' rather than the proof. Supporters still regard the panel as a possible record, and park interpretation presents it with caveats.
entries.source_note: Krupp, Journal of Skyscape Archaeology 1.2 (2015); NPS Chaco page.

claims.claim: An 'orb of extraordinary brilliance' at the hour of Leo IX's death in Rome; read by some as the supernova in the evening sky, by most as a conventional sign or a planet
claims.evidence: Tractatus de ecclesia S. Petri Aldenburgensi; Collins et al. 1999

claims.claim: Guest star at the hour of the ox (c. 2 a.m.) in the east, in the lodges Shi and Shen, flaring at Tianguan, as large as Jupiter; month probably an error for the 5th
Guest star in the lodge Mao (Pleiades) linked to a midday solar eclipse; dated by rival readings to May 1054, Nov 1053 or Jan 1055
claims.evidence: Qidan guozhi; Ho et al. 1972; Breen and McCarthy 1995

claims.claim: Variant day yichou (10 June) in the Changbian; most read it as a slip for jichou (4 July)
First seen at dawn in the east, 'several inches' (cun) SE of Tianguan (zeta Tauri), i.e. guarding it from below
Visible in daylight like Venus, rays on four sides, reddish-white; seen by day 23 days in all
Calculated: waning crescent Moon about 2 degrees from the new star low in the east; proposed as the scene of the Peñasco Blanco panel
'Spectacular star' in Gemini coinciding with epidemics in Constantinople (c.14,000 buried) and Egypt; star treated as accompanying corrupted air
Faint yellow glow about the star; does not trespass on the lodge Bi; omen of a person of great worth in the realm
Guest star no longer visible, after about 642 days; 'omen of the departure of the guest'
claims.evidence: Song shi basic annals; Song huiyao

claims.claim: Nebula above the southern horn of Taurus: no stars, whitish light like a candle flame; position measured, becomes M1
Filamentary oval drawn with a 36-inch reflector; the drawing gives the name 'Crab'
The 1054 guest star was recorded close to NGC 1952 (M1)
Expansion of the nebula traced back gives an age of about 900 years, matching 1054
Daylight visibility, 642-day span, distance and expansion imply a supernova; Crab = remnant of 1054 star
No primary star-and-crescent rock image is a satisfactory depiction of the 1054 supernova; Peñasco Blanco may post-date the 12th century

convergences.label: Pope Leo IX dies in Rome
convergences.note: A Flemish text sets a brilliant orb over his death; his legates in Constantinople went on acting in his name without knowing he was dead, which Cerularius later used against them. One event, read as a sky sign in the West and as a legal flaw in the East.

convergences.label: The first sighting: May, June or July?
convergences.note: The Japanese archive says the 4th month, one Song compilation says yichou (10 June), the Liao text points to an eclipse, and the main Song record says jichou (4 July). Laid side by side, the records show how a single copying slip can move a date by weeks.

convergences.label: Dawn: the guest star by Tianguan
convergences.note: Kaifeng logs the star at dawn in the east beside Tianguan; the Japanese note, also of a pre-dawn eastern sighting at Tianguan, compares it to Jupiter. Both are bureau records transmitted through later books, and both place it at the same star.

convergences.label: The old Moon beside the new star
convergences.note: On the morning after the Song first sighting, the crescent Moon stood close to the star in the east. The Song astronomers do not mention it; the Peñasco Blanco panel may or may not show it. One of these is a dated text, the other an undated image.

convergences.label: The bull on the altar of Hagia Sophia
convergences.note: In Constantinople the legates excommunicate the patriarch at mid-morning; in Kaifeng, about five and a half hours of longitude east, the star is in its thirteenth day of daylight visibility. Ibn Butlan, in the same city, wrote of the star and the plague but not of the schism; the churchmen wrote of the schism but not of the star.

convergences.label: The synod answers the bull
convergences.note: Cerularius' synod anathematizes the departed legates on 20 July and proclaims it on the 24th. Humbert is at sea; Ibn Butlan, whose Eucharist treatise served the patriarch's side, is still in the city in the epidemic year he dated by the star.

convergences.label: An omen of worth, sent to the historians
convergences.note: Yang Weide reads the star as a blessing on Renzong's reign and the court congratulates the emperor; a few weeks earlier the star had been in daylight over a church council that tore Christendom. The same light carried a favourable meaning in one capital and none at all in the other.

convergences.label: Kaifeng's notes reach the Astronomical Society of the Pacific
convergences.note: Duyvendak's translations of the Song bureau and Yang Weide appear beside Mayall and Oort's analysis, completing a chain that ran from Messier's catalogue and Rosse's drawing through Lundmark's hint and Hubble's expansion age. Records kept for omen-reading became evidence for stellar physics.

ties.note: Ibn Butlan wrote his Eucharist treatise in spring 1054 at the instance of the patriarch's circle, supporting the Greek position on leavened bread.
Humbert's bull of 16 July excommunicated Cerularius; Cerularius' synod of 20 July anathematized Humbert and his fellow legates.
Both were in Constantinople in the spring and summer of 1054 and wrote on the same Eucharist controversy from opposite sides; no meeting is recorded.
The Oudenburg text centres on the death of Leo IX, the pope who had sent Humbert's legation; his death undercut the legates' authority.
Yang Weide was a senior figure of the astronomical office whose dawn reports he interpreted; his memorial was copied into the same compilation as the bureau's observations.
Rival courts bound by the treaty of 1005; each watched the same lodges of Taurus and read the star for its own ruler.
Both copied the 1054 note from the Onmyōryō archive on separate occasions, which is why they share the doubtful 'fourth month'.
Rosse turned his large reflectors on objects from Messier's catalogue; his drawing of M1 gave Messier's first object its popular name.
Lundmark worked from nineteenth-century European translations of Chinese guest-star lists derived from the Song records.
Hubble's 1928 identification built on the proximity Lundmark had noted and on the 1921 expansion measurements.
Duyvendak's 1942 translation brought Yang Weide's memorial into the astronomical literature, where it is still cited.
Mayall and Oort tested and extended Hubble's suggestion with a full analysis of brightness, distance and expansion.

threads_out.note: Twelve years later the Song astronomers, the Liao and Japanese courts and European chroniclers all recorded Halley's comet in April 1066; at Peñasco Blanco the faint tailed rings above the hand have been speculatively read as that comet, and Messier found M1 while hunting Halley's predicted return in 1758.

The excommunications of July 1054 became the conventional date of the split between the Latin and Greek churches; the failed union of Florence (1439) and the Latin aid that did not save Constantinople in 1453 were played out against that breach.

The Japanese record of the 1054 star came from the archive of the Heian court's Onmyōryō, the Bureau of Yin and Yang whose diviners appear throughout Heian court diaries; Teika's family descended from the Fujiwara regents of that court.

The remnant of the 1054 star is invisible to the naked eye; only the telescope, from Bevis and Messier to Rosse's great reflectors and the photographic plates of Mount Wilson and Lick, made the nebula and its expansion visible and so allowed it to be dated.

vantage_key: 0 = the Song court astronomers who watched and interpreted the star; 1 = other possible eyewitness records (Liao court, Ibn Butlan, the disputed European and Chaco candidates); 2 = churchmen in Constantinople on the same days who did not mention the sky; 3 = Japanese compilers copying the record generations later; 4 = modern astronomers who catalogued the remnant and identified it with 1054.
